goals: Name the parts of a spherical mirror and use f = R/2
Draw the reflected ray for each of the specific incident rays
Draw simple ray diagrams for a concave mirror and state the position, nature and size of the image for each object position

slides.heading: Mirrors that curve
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a curved mirror can gather light into a point or spread it out, depending on which side shines.

visual.alt: Flow from a part of a hollow sphere to the concave and convex mirrors

slides.narration: A shiny spoon shows your face upside down on one side and upright on the other. That is because a spoon is a curved mirror, and the two sides are a concave and a convex surface.

slides.heading: The parts of a spherical mirror
slides.body_md: A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere. Its middle point is the **pole P**. The centre of the sphere is the **centre of curvature C**, and the **radius of curvature R** is the distance PC. The line PC is the **principal axis**. The **principal focus F** is where rays parallel to the axis meet, and the **focal length f** is the distance PF.

visual.alt: A concave mirror with the pole, focus, centre of curvature, principal axis, R and f marked

slides.narration: The pole is the middle of the mirror. The centre of the sphere it came from is the centre of curvature. The line joining them is the principal axis. The focus lies halfway between the pole and the centre.

slides.heading: Concave and convex; f = R/2
slides.body_md: In a **concave** mirror the reflecting surface curves **inwards**; it **converges** parallel rays to a **real** focus in front. In a **convex** mirror the surface bulges **outwards**; it **diverges** parallel rays, which appear to come from a **virtual** focus behind it. For both, the focal length is **half** the radius of curvature: $f = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table comparing a concave mirror and a convex mirror

slides.narration: A concave mirror curves inwards like the inside of a bowl, and it brings parallel rays together. A convex mirror bulges outwards and spreads rays apart. In both cases the focal length is half the radius of curvature.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: f from R
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Find the focal length of each.

**Step 1.** Concave: $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{30}{2} = 15$ cm (in the sign convention, $f = -15$ cm).

**Step 2.** Convex: $f = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20$ cm (in the sign convention, $f = +20$ cm).

visual.alt: Table of the radius of curvature and the focal length of a concave and a convex mirror

slides.narration: Divide the radius of curvature by two. The concave mirror has a focal length of fifteen centimetres and the convex mirror has twenty centimetres. Later we will give the concave one a negative sign.

slides.body_md: Use f = R ÷ 2.

slides.heading: Specific rays: parallel to the axis and through F
slides.body_md: We draw images using rays whose path we know. **A ray parallel to the principal axis** is reflected **through F** (concave) or **as if from F** (convex). **A ray through F** (or directed towards F) is reflected **parallel to the axis**. **A ray through C** (or towards C) is reflected **straight back** along its own path.

slides.narration: In the diagram a beam parallel to the axis is reflected through the focus. The reverse also holds: a ray through the focus comes back parallel to the axis. A ray directed through the centre of curvature returns along its own path.

slides.heading: A parallel beam at an angle
slides.body_md: A beam of **parallel rays at a small angle to the axis** is reflected so that the rays meet at a point **Q** on the **focal plane**, the plane through F at **right angles** to the principal axis. A very distant object gives parallel rays, so its image lies **at the focus**: for an object at infinity the image is formed at F.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: where is the object?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A concave mirror has $f = -12$ cm. An object is 30 cm in front of it. In which region is the object, and where is the image?

**Step 1.** $R = 2f = -24$ cm, so C is 24 cm from the pole. The object at 30 cm is **beyond C**.

**Step 2.** The image is real and between F and C. By the formula, $v = -20$ cm, which is between 12 cm and 24 cm in front.

slides.heading: Why a convex mirror cannot give a real image
slides.body_md: A convex mirror **diverges** all rays. Reflected rays never meet in front of the mirror, so **no real image** can form. Only their **backward extensions** meet, behind the mirror, which gives a **virtual** image. Since the rays spread, the image is always **smaller** than the object.

slides.heading: Uses of concave and convex mirrors
slides.body_md: A **concave** mirror with the object **inside F** gives an **enlarged, erect** image: **shaving and make-up mirrors**, dentists’ mirrors. slides.heading: The Cartesian sign convention
slides.body_md: The **pole is the origin**. Light travels **from left to right**, and the object is always on the left. Distances **against** the direction of the incident light are **negative**; along it, **positive**. Heights **above** the principal axis are **positive**, below it negative.

slides.narration: Remember: a concave mirror has a negative focal length and a convex mirror has a positive focal length. The object distance is always negative. A real image is in front, so its distance is negative too.

slides.heading: The mirror formula and magnification
slides.body_md: For a mirror, $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$. The **magnification** is the ratio of image height to object height: $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$. A **negative m** means an **inverted** (real) image, a **positive m** an **erect** (virtual) one. $|m| > 1$ means enlarged, $|m| < 1$ diminished. We use the formula without proof.

slides.narration: The reciprocal of the image distance plus the reciprocal of the object distance equals the reciprocal of the focal length. The magnification is minus the image distance divided by the object distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a concave mirror
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A concave mirror has $f = -15$ cm. An object 4 cm tall is placed 25 cm in front of it. Find $v$, $m$ and the height of the image.

**Step 1.** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-15} - \dfrac{1}{-25}$, so $v = -37.5$ cm: a real image in front of the mirror.

**Step 2.** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-37.5}{-25} = -1.5$, so $h' = m h = -1.5 \times 4 = -6$ cm: **inverted**, 6 cm tall.

**Problem.** A convex mirror has $f = +20$ cm. An object 6 cm tall is 60 cm in front of it. Find $v$, $m$ and the height of the image.

**Step 2.** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{15}{-60} = +0.25$, so $h' = 0.25 \times 6 = 1.5$ cm: erect and diminished.

notes.title: Spherical Mirrors — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Concave and convex mirrors; pole, centre of curvature, focus; f = R/2
sections.body_md:
A **spherical mirror** is a part of a hollow sphere whose one surface is silvered. If the **inner** (hollow) surface reflects, it is a **concave** (converging) mirror; if the **outer** (bulging) surface reflects, it is a **convex** (diverging) mirror.

- **Pole (P):** the middle point of the mirror surface.
- **Centre of curvature (C):** the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part. **Radius of curvature (R):** the radius of that sphere, R = PC.
- **Principal axis:** the straight line through P and C.
- **Principal focus (F):** the point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave: real focus in front) or from which they appear to come (convex: virtual focus behind). **Focal length (f):** the distance PF.
- **f = R/2** is used without proof. For a concave mirror f and R are negative in the Cartesian convention, for a convex mirror positive.

The derivation of f = R/2 and of the mirror formula is not required in Class IX.

key_terms.definition_md: The middle point of the surface of a spherical mirror.
The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.
The point on the principal axis at which rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to meet (convex) after reflection.
The distance between the pole and the principal focus.

sections.heading: 2. Paths of specific rays
sections.body_md:
Three rays whose paths are known are used to draw images:

1. A ray **parallel to the principal axis** is reflected **through F** (concave) or **as if coming from F** (convex).
2. A ray **through F** (concave), or directed **towards F** (convex), is reflected **parallel to the principal axis**.
3. A ray **through C**, or directed **towards C**, falls along the normal and is reflected **back along its own path**.

**Parallel rays meeting on the focal plane:** a beam of parallel rays at a small angle to the principal axis is reflected so that the rays meet at a point on the **focal plane** (the plane through F perpendicular to the principal axis). A very distant object gives parallel rays, so its image lies **at F**.

Ray diagrams in this chapter are simple sketches; **scale drawing and graphical construction are removed topics**.

key_terms.definition_md: The plane through the principal focus at right angles to the principal axis.

rows: Through F (concave); appears to come from F (convex)

sections.heading: 3. Images formed by a concave mirror
sections.body_md:
The image depends on where the object is placed.

| Object | Image position | Nature | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F | Real, inverted | Highly diminished (a point) |
| Beyond C | Between F and C | Real, inverted | diminished |
| At C | At C | Real, inverted | same size |
| Between C and F | Beyond C | Real, inverted | enlarged |
| At F | At infinity | Real, inverted | highly enlarged |
| Between F and P | Behind the mirror | Virtual, erect | enlarged |

The sizes follow from the mirror formula (for f = −10 cm, magnifications -0.5, -1, -2 and +2 for u = −30, −20, −15 and −5 cm). A **real** image can be caught on a screen and is inverted; a **virtual** image cannot and is erect. Draw each diagram with two of the rays of section 2.

An image formed where the reflected rays only appear to meet; it cannot be received on a screen.

sections.heading: 4. The convex mirror; uses of mirrors
sections.body_md:
**Image in a convex mirror:** for every position of the object the image is **virtual, erect and diminished** and lies **between P and F, behind the mirror**. The rays diverge after reflection and only their backward extensions meet, so no real image can form; as the object moves far away the image moves towards F, and its size decreases.

**Uses of a concave mirror**
- **Shaving mirror, make-up mirror, dentist's mirror:** the object is inside F, so the image is erect and enlarged.
- **Torch, car headlight:** the lamp is at F, so the reflected light is a parallel beam.
- **Solar cooker or furnace:** parallel sunlight is focused at F.

**Uses of a convex mirror**
- **Rear-view mirror of a vehicle:** the image is erect and the **field of view is wide**.
- **Street light reflector, security mirror in a shop:** a wide area is covered.

key_terms.definition_md: The extent of the region that can be seen in a mirror.

rows: Lamp at F gives a parallel beam
Erect image with a wide field of view

sections.heading: 5. Cartesian sign convention; the mirror formula and magnification
sections.body_md:
**Cartesian sign convention** (used throughout)
- The **pole** is the origin and the **principal axis** is the x-axis; light travels from left to right and the object is placed on the left.
- Distances measured **against** the direction of the incident light (to the left of P) are **negative**; **along** it (to the right of P) are **positive**.
- Heights **above** the principal axis are **positive**; below it, negative.
- Therefore **u is negative** for a real object; **f and R are negative for a concave mirror** and **positive for a convex mirror**; **v is negative for a real image** of a concave mirror and **positive for a virtual image**.

**Mirror formula and magnification** (used without derivation; direct numericals only)
$$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \qquad m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$$
A **negative m** means an inverted (real) image, a **positive m** an erect (virtual) image; $|m| > 1$ enlarged, $|m| < 1$ diminished.

**Worked check.** Concave mirror, f = -15 cm, u = -25 cm, object 4 cm tall: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives v = -37.5 cm (real, in front), m = -1.5, image -6 cm (inverted).

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, m = h′/h = −v/u.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the wrong sign convention: u is negative, f is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror.
- Drawing the image of a convex mirror in front of the mirror, or a real image with dotted lines.
- Leaving out arrows on rays, or the dotted backward extensions for virtual images.
- Forgetting that m is negative for an inverted image and quoting v without its sign.
- Teaching or using scale drawing or the derivation of the mirror formula: both are removed from Class IX.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Ray diagrams (2 to 3 marks): two rays with arrows, correct position of the image, labels P, F, C.
- Image description (2 marks): position, nature, size.
- Numericals (2 to 3 marks): sign convention, formula with substitution, answer with sign and unit.
- Uses (2 marks): the mirror and the reason (shaving mirror inside F, rear-view mirror wide field).

questions.stem_md: Why is a convex mirror preferred to a plane mirror as the rear-view mirror of a car?

answer.model_answer_md: A convex mirror forms an **erect, diminished image**, so it covers a **much wider field of view** than a plane mirror of the same size, and the driver can see more of the road behind.

questions.solution_md: Erect diminished image gives a wider field of view than a plane mirror.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.

answer.model_answer_md: A convex mirror **diverges** every ray that falls on it. The reflected rays never meet in front of the mirror, so **no real image** is formed. Their backward extensions meet **behind the mirror**, between the pole and the focus, which gives a **virtual, erect** image, and as the rays spread out the image is **smaller** than the object.

questions.solution_md: Rays diverge, so no real image; backward extensions meet behind between P and F, giving a small virtual image.

questions.stem_md:
A concave mirror has a focal length of 15 cm. An object 6 cm tall is placed 45 cm in front of the mirror.

(a) State the signs of f and u in the Cartesian sign convention. [2]

(b) Find the image distance. [2]

(c) Find the magnification. [2]

(d) Find the height of the image and state whether the image is real or virtual, and erect or inverted. [2]

(e) State whether the object is between F and C, or beyond C. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Both are **negative**: $f = -15$ cm (concave mirror) and $u = -45$ cm (object in front).

**(b)** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{45} = -\dfrac{2}{45}$, so $v = -22.5$ cm.

**(c)** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-22.5}{-45} = -0.5$.

**(d)** $h' = m h = -0.5 \times 6 = -3$ cm. The image is **real** (v is negative) and **inverted** (m is negative).

**(e)** $R = 2f = -30$ cm, so C is 30 cm from the mirror; the object at 45 cm is **beyond C**.

questions.solution_md: f and u negative; −22.5 cm; −0.5; −3 cm, real and inverted; beyond C.

questions.stem_md:
A concave shaving mirror has a focal length of 18 cm. A small pimple 3 mm high is 12 cm from the mirror.

(a) State whether the pimple is between F and P, or beyond F. [1]

(b) Find the image distance. [2]

(c) Find the magnification. [2]

(d) Find the height of the image in mm. [1]

(e) State the nature of the image (real or virtual, erect or inverted, enlarged or diminished). [2]

(f) Why is a concave mirror, and not a plane mirror, used for shaving? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The mirror's F is 18 cm from P and the pimple is 12 cm from P, so it is **between F and P**.

**(b)** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{18} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{36}$, so $v = +36$ cm.

**(c)** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{36}{-12} = +3$.

**(d)** $h' = m h = 3 \times 3 = 9$ mm.

**(e)** **Virtual** (v positive), **erect** (m positive) and **enlarged** (m greater than 1).

**(f)** A concave mirror with the face inside F gives an **enlarged, erect image**, so details of the skin are seen clearly; a plane mirror gives only an image of the same size.

questions.solution_md: Between F and P; +36 cm; +3; 9 mm; virtual, erect, enlarged; enlarged erect image.

marking_scheme.step: Concave mirror gives an enlarged image
Plane mirror gives the same size

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows an object in front of a convex mirror and the image formed. The focal length of the mirror is 40 cm, and an object is placed 120 cm in front of it.

(a) Find the radius of curvature of the mirror. [1]

(b) Find the image distance, with its sign. [2]

(c) Find the magnification. [2]

(d) State the position, nature and size of the image. [3]

(e) Name one use of a convex mirror and give the reason for it. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $R = 2f = 2 \times 40 = 80$ cm.

**(b)** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{40} + \dfrac{1}{120} = \dfrac{4}{120}$, so $v = +30$ cm.

**(c)** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{30}{-120} = +0.25$.

**(d)** The image is **behind the mirror**, at 30 cm from the pole (between P and F); it is **virtual and erect**; and **diminished** to one quarter of the size of the object.

**(e)** A **rear-view mirror**: it gives an erect image and a **wide field of view**.

questions.stem_md:
A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of it.

(a) Find the focal length, with its sign. [1]

(b) State whether the object is beyond C, between C and F, or between F and P. [1]

(c) Find the image distance. [2]

(d) Find the magnification. [2]

(e) Find the height of the image, and say whether it is erect or inverted. [2]

(f) State whether the image can be obtained on a screen, with a reason. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{-40}{2} = -20$ cm.

**(b)** C is 40 cm from the mirror and F is 20 cm from it; the object at 30 cm is **between C and F**.

**(c)** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = -60$ cm.

**(d)** $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-60}{-30} = -2$.

**(e)** $h' = m h = -2 \times 5 = -10$ cm, so the image is 10 cm tall and **inverted**.

**(f)** **Yes**, because v is negative, so the image is **real**: the reflected rays actually meet there, so it can be received on a screen 60 cm in front of the mirror.

questions.solution_md: −20 cm; between C and F; −60 cm; −2; 10 cm inverted; real image so it can be received on a screen.

questions.stem_md: A concave mirror forms a real image that is twice as tall as the object when the object is 15 cm in front of the mirror. Find the focal length of the mirror, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: A real image is inverted, so $m = -2 = -\dfrac{v}{u}$ with $u = -15$ cm, which gives $v = -30$ cm. Then $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $f = -10$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A pin placed 24 cm in front of a concave mirror has its real image formed at the same place as the pin. Find the focal length of the mirror, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: $u = v = -24$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{1}{24} = -\dfrac{1}{12}$, so $f = -12$ cm (the pin is at the centre of curvature).
